extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and problem-solvers studying elementary number theory and combinatorics (olympiad/contest level)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, heuristics and standard criteria used in solving Diophantine equations, modular contradictions, divisibility/parity arguments, combinatorial constructions, and matching problems as presented in an elementary number theory & combinatorics textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce to primitive solutions by dividing out gcd
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume gcd(x, y, z, ...) = 1 (or remove common factors) to reduce to primitive solutions before deriving contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many solutions begin by assuming a common divisor does not divide all variables (or dividing it out) because otherwise one can produce a smaller solution; this is used to reach contradictions about divisibility (examples: Problems 3.64, 3.65, 3.66). Anti-pattern: ignoring common factors can hide infinite descent or scaling arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check residues modulo small primes (modular contradictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use congruences and the set of possible residues of powers modulo a chosen modulus to rule out solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: square residues modulo 7 are {0,1,2,4} so two squares adding to 0 (mod 7) force both 0 (Problem 3.64/3.64 solution); squares modulo 8 are {0,1,4} used to rule out sums equaling 7 (Problem 3.68). Choose modulus p to expose impossible residue combinations. Include computation of residues and check all combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Fermat’s little theorem to limit power residues (choose p = 2k+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term x^k appears and p = 2k + 1 is prime, check the equation modulo p since x^k can only take values -1, 0, 1 (mod p) when p ∤ x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook explicitly advises: 'if in a Diophantine equation we have a term like x^k and p = 2k+1 is a prime number, it is a good idea to check the equation mod p.' Example: choosing p = 19 for x^9 terms reduces possible residues to ±1,0 and helps rule out cases (Problem 3.69/Observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity and 2-adic valuation arguments (factor out powers of 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze parity (even/odd) and repeatedly divide by 2 when both sides or variables are even to derive contradictions or reduce exponents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common pattern: if x,y both even, divide by 2 to get smaller solution; factor (x^m - y^m)(x^m + y^m) = 2^k forces both factors to be powers of 2, giving parity restrictions (Problem 3.65). Use mod 4 observations (e.g., 3 ≡ -1 (mod 4) implies 3^{2k}+1 ≡ 2 (mod 4)) as in Problem 3.78.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization of differences/polynomials to deduce structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor expressions like x^n - y^n or algebraic factorizations to split an equation into factors whose divisibility properties can be analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: write x^n - y^n = (x-y)(...) to force the second factor odd when n odd (Problem 3.65); factor 2^{ab}-1 into cyclotomic-like factors to reason about compositeness or construct many factors (Problems 3.75–3.77). Use parity/gcd constraints on factors to reach contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction via divisibility by a specific prime (forcing all variables divisible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that a particular prime must divide certain variables (often all), contradicting primitivity/gcd = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show z,t divisible by 7 from residue constraints, then deduce x,y also divisible by 7 contradicting gcd = 1 (Problem 3.64). Approach: demonstrate residues force multiple variables ≡ 0 (mod p).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding/inequality arguments to show impossibility (size comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use inequalities and growth-rate comparisons to show an algebraic condition (like being a square) cannot hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Problem 3.66 derive inequalities showing a constructed expression lies strictly between consecutive squares, so it cannot be a perfect square. Use asymptotic or explicit term comparisons to rule out square-ness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary variables (a,b,c) and analyze gcds/divisibility structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose a complicated rational/integer expression into simpler integer factors a,b,c and study their gcds and divisibility to conclude about square-ness or parity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: set a=x^{1000}+1, b=x^{500}+1, c=(x^{500}-1)/(x-1) and argue their gcds ≤ 2 and therefore product abc being a square forces each to be squares or twice squares, leading to contradiction (Problem 3.66).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use polynomial/algebraic expansions to bound or restrict variable values
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand binomials or manipulate polynomial identities (e.g., (x-1)^4 expansion) to produce inequalities or term-by-term comparisons that restrict variable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: expand (x_k - 1)^4 to bound x_k and conclude x_k ∈ {1,2} in Problem 3.67. Use expansion to produce sums of nonnegative terms and compare to small constants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digit-sum modulo 9 lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integer n with digit sum s(n), the difference n - s(n) is divisible by 9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma: n - s(n) = Σ a_i(10^i - 1) is divisible by 9 because each 10^i - 1 ≡ 0 (mod 9). Used to show rearranged decimal digits of powers of 2 cannot produce multiples dividing by 9 (Problem 3.81) and in comparing digital sums (Problem 3.82).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use periodicity/orders of residues (powers of 2 modulo small moduli)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the known periodic remainders of 2^n modulo small numbers (e.g., modulo 5 or 9) to deduce divisibility or digital-sum behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: powers of 2 modulo 5 cycle with period 4 used in Problem 3.83; remainders modulo 9 (sequence 2,4,8,7,5,1) and periodicity 6 used in Problem 3.82 to obtain growth contradictions for digit sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive existence via induction (build numbers/sequences meeting digit/divisibility constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove existence by inductively appending digits or constructing next-case from previous, ensuring divisibility properties are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: build numbers with n digits each 1 or 2 divisible by 2^n (Problem 3.79), and construct sets of binary strings with Hamming-distance constraints inductively (Problem 3.80). Give base cases and two-case inductive step depending on divisibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole / counting arguments for combinatorial impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use counting of coincidences, pigeonhole principle, or simple counting bounds to get contradictions or bounds on the number of possible objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bounding total digit coincidences in Problem 3.80; partitioning integers into two sets with deliberate gaps so neither contains long arithmetic progression (Problem 3.92); counting terms ≤ N in arithmetic progressions to derive Σ (1/ri) = 1 (Problem 3.96).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cauchy–Schwarz (or quadratic inequalities) to relate sums of absolute differences and squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to compare Σ|xi - xj|^2 and Σ(xi - xj)^2 and characterize equality cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.101: after normalizing (add constant to make mean zero) apply Cauchy–Schwarz to show inequality and deduce equality iff the xi form an arithmetic progression. Technique: rewrite LHS/RHS in forms suitable for Cauchy–Schwarz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use integer/root theorems on polynomials to deduce integrality of sequence parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Show a parameter is an integer by demonstrating it is an integer root of a polynomial with integer coefficients (rational/integer root theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Problem 3.99 rewrite condition as P(a1) = 0 for polynomial P with integer coefficients; by integer root theorem conclude a1 ∈ Z then deduce common difference integral and thus all terms are integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model combinatorial constraints as bipartite matching problems (apply Hall’s marriage lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate rows/columns/items into a bipartite graph of 'boys' and 'girls' with acquaintances defined by presence/compatibility; verify Hall’s condition to deduce existence of a matching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: card-selection from columns to get all denominations (Problem 3.104), permuting columns to form Latin-rectangle rows (Problem 3.110), selecting positive entries in stochastic matrices (Problem 3.108). Guidance: define acquaintance relation, count neighborhoods, and apply Hall's theorem. When Hall fails, extract the violating set to produce an alternate conclusion (Problem 3.105, 3.109).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove nonexistence by checking small residue sets and counting possible residues (exclude specific residues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute possible residues of each term modulo a chosen prime and check the target residue is impossible (often by enumerating allowed residues of squares/powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for x^5 = y^2 + 4 check modulo 11 (Problem 3.71) and enumerate residues of fifth powers and squares to see no equality is possible; for Problem 3.69 enumerate possible residues modulo 19 and show RHS ≡ 14 which is unattainable by LHS residues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use construction via algebraic identities to interleave/provide sequences with desired order properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Create explicit real/integer sequences (arithmetical/geometric) using algebraic truncation or binomial-like constructions so that inequalities between terms hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 3.98 constructs B_k = (1 + 1/m)^k and A_k = 1 + k + 1/2 to ensure B1 < A1 < B2 < A2 < ... and then scales to integer sequences. Strategy: choose large m and scale to integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor large numbers into many large factors by repeated difference-of-powers factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Write expressions like a^m - 1 as product of factors a^{d} ± 1 to produce many factors exceeding a given bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 3.77 factors 2^{1992} - 1 using 2^{2249·8} - 1 = (2^{2249} - 1)(2^{2249} + 1)... and further factor terms into sums/differences to obtain six factors each > 2248. Technique: use exponent factorizations and algebraic identities recursively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit periodicity/structure of powers (orders) to create eventual constancy mod n
rubrics_metrics.description: Show sequences like 2, 22, 222, ... modulo n are eventually constant by using factorization properties and Euler’s theorem on reduced modulo parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.88: define x_{m+1} = 2 x_m and show for n = 2^a b (b odd) that for k ≥ n one has x_k ≡ x_{k+1} (mod 2^a) and reduce modulo b by induction using φ(b) ≤ n - 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple combinatorial constructions with factorial denominators to produce rationals with given numerator denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce rational sequences with certain fractional parts or denominators, use terms 1/n!, 2/n!, ..., n/n! and reduce to lowest terms to land in a bounded set of rationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 3.100: to show A = {1,1/2,1/3,...} contains arithmetic sequences of given length use multiples of 1/n!; boundedness implies no infinite arithmetic progression. Technique: scale by factorial to ensure denominators divide and reduce.
